title: Unit 2 Quiz · Statistics for Data Science
instructions: 33 questions, 36 marks. You have 30 minutes; the quiz submits itself when time runs out.
Keep a rough sheet and a calculator ready: several questions need a quick calculation.
Questions and options are shuffled, so your neighbour's screen will not match yours.
Multi-select questions need ALL correct options for the marks. Ordering questions give part marks for each item in the right place.
After submitting you will see your score and an explanation for every question.

questions.q: KiranaMart weighs 40 atta packets and uses the result to decide whether ALL packets from the machine are under-filled. This is an example of:
questions.explain: Using a sample to draw a conclusion about the whole population is inferential statistics. Descriptive statistics only summarise the data you actually have.

questions.q: The average weight of the 40 packets that were weighed (995.4 g) is a:
questions.explain: A number calculated from a sample is a statistic. The true average of every packet the machine fills (μ) is the parameter, and we usually never know it exactly.

questions.q: A customer rating from 1★ to 5★ is which level of measurement?
questions.explain: Ratings have a clear order (5★ is better than 4★) but the gaps are not guaranteed to be equal, so they are ordinal.

questions.q: Items in seven orders: 1, 2, 2, 3, 2, 5, 6. What are the mean, median and mode?
questions.explain: Sum = 21, so mean = 21 / 7 = 3. Sorted: 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 5, 6, so the middle (4th) value, the median, is 2. 2 appears most often, so the mode is 2.

questions.q: For the values 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 (mean = 5), what is the POPULATION standard deviation (divide by n)?
questions.explain: Squared deviations: 9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4, 16 → sum 32. Variance = 32 / 8 = 4, so σ = √4 = 2. (Dividing by n − 1 = 7 gives the sample SD, 2.14.)

questions.q: In the delivery trial, the mean order value is ₹685 and the median is ₹620. What does this tell you about the distribution?
options: It is right-skewed: a few large orders pull the mean up
It is left-skewed: a few tiny orders pull the mean down
questions.explain: When mean > median, a long tail of large values is dragging the mean to the right. The skewness of order value is +2.47.

questions.q: You want to report the 'typical' monthly income in a town where a few people are billionaires. Which measure of centre is the best choice?
questions.explain: The median is resistant to extreme values; the mean would be pulled far up by a few billionaires. Range and variance measure spread, not centre.

questions.q: What does this code print, and why?
questions.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
x = [10, 20, 30]
print(round(np.std(x), 2), pd.Series(x).std())
options: 8.16 10.0: NumPy divides by n by default, pandas by n − 1
10.0 8.16: NumPy divides by n − 1, pandas by n
questions.explain: Squared deviations sum to 200. NumPy (ddof=0): √(200/3) = 8.16. pandas (ddof=1): √(200/2) = 10.0. Use ddof=1 in NumPy for the sample SD.

questions.q: Delivery time is roughly normal with mean 31.4 min and SD 6.4 min. About 95% of deliveries take between:
questions.explain: 95% lies within ±2 SD: 31.4 ± 12.8 = 18.6 to 44.2. ±1 SD (25.0 to 37.8) holds about 68%, ±3 SD about 99.7%. The real data had 96.2% within ±2 SD.

questions.q: With mean 31.4 min and SD 6.4 min, what is the z-score of a 45-minute delivery?
questions.explain: z = (45 − 31.4) / 6.4 = 13.6 / 6.4 ≈ 2.13. It is 2.13 standard deviations ABOVE the mean, so the z-score is positive.

questions.q: Select ALL the true properties of a normal distribution.
options: Mean, median and mode are equal
The total area under the curve is 1
It is always skewed to the right
questions.explain: The normal curve is symmetric around the mean, so mean = median = mode, and like every probability curve its total area is 1. A skewed distribution is by definition NOT normal.

questions.q: A delivery has a z-score of 0. What does that mean?
options: It took exactly the mean time
questions.explain: z measures distance from the mean in SD units. z = 0 means zero distance: the value equals the mean.

questions.q: In the trial, ExpressGo delivered 184 orders and 30 of them were late (over 40 min). Overall, 52 of 600 orders were late. What is P(late | ExpressGo)?
questions.explain: Conditional probability looks only inside the ExpressGo group: 30 / 184 ≈ 0.163 (16.3%). 52/600 = 0.087 is the overall rate; 30/52 = 0.577 is P(ExpressGo | late).

questions.q: Each packet is under-weight with probability 0.2, independently of other packets. What is the probability that two randomly picked packets are BOTH under-weight?
questions.explain: For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) = 0.2 × 0.2 = 0.04.

questions.q: The team splits customers into 'New' and 'Returning' and then randomly picks 50 customers from each group for a survey. Which sampling method is this?
questions.explain: Dividing the population into groups (strata) and sampling randomly from EACH group is stratified sampling. Cluster sampling picks whole groups.

questions.q: Order values have population SD σ = ₹350. What is the standard error of the mean for samples of n = 49 orders?
questions.explain: SE = 350 / √49 = 350 / 7 = ₹50. Dividing by n (49) instead of √n gives the wrong answer 7.14.

questions.q: Order values are strongly right-skewed. What does the Central Limit Theorem say about the means of many samples of 30 orders?
options: Their distribution is approximately normal, centred on the population mean
Their distribution is just as skewed as the original data
Every sample mean equals the population mean exactly
Sample means cannot be used for inference when data is skewed
questions.explain: The CLT says sample means are approximately normal for large enough n (≈30+), whatever the shape of the population, with mean μ and SD σ/√n. In the lab, 2,000 sample means formed a bell around ₹685.

questions.q: The team wants to know whether the new route app changes delivery time. What is the null hypothesis H₀?
options: The mean delivery time is the same with the old and new app
The sample means are exactly equal
questions.explain: H₀ is always the 'no effect / no difference' statement about the POPULATIONS (μ_old = μ_new). The claim we want evidence for goes in H₁.

questions.q: Which is the correct meaning of a p-value?
options: The probability of getting a result at least this extreme IF the null hypothesis is true
The probability that the null hypothesis is true
The probability that the alternative hypothesis is true
The size of the difference between the groups
questions.explain: The p-value assumes H₀ is true and asks how surprising our data would be. A small p means the data would be very unusual under H₀. It is NOT the probability that H₀ is true.

questions.q: A test gives p = 0.03 with significance level α = 0.05. What is the decision?
options: Change α to 0.01 so the result fits
questions.explain: p (0.03) < α (0.05), so the result is statistically significant and we reject H₀. Choosing α after seeing the data is cheating.

questions.q: The packing machine is actually fine, but your test concludes it is under-filling and the line is stopped for nothing. This is a:
questions.explain: Rejecting a TRUE null hypothesis is a Type I error, a false alarm. Its probability is α. Missing a real problem (not rejecting a false H₀) is a Type II error.

questions.q: Arrange the steps of a hypothesis test in the correct order.
options: Choose the test and compute the test statistic
Compare p with α, decide and explain it in business terms
questions.explain: Hypotheses → α (decided BEFORE looking at results) → test statistic → p-value → decision and plain-language conclusion.

questions.q: You want to compare the mean delivery time of THREE delivery partners. Which test fits?
questions.explain: One numeric variable compared across three or more groups → one-way ANOVA. Running many T-tests instead would inflate the chance of a false positive.

questions.q: Is payment mode (UPI / Card / COD) related to customer type (New / Returning)? Which test fits?
questions.explain: Both variables are categorical, so we compare observed and expected COUNTS in a contingency table with the chi-square test.

questions.q: When should you use a T-test instead of a Z-test for a mean?
options: When the population standard deviation is unknown (especially with small samples)
When there are more than two groups
When the sample is very large and σ is known
questions.explain: The Z-test needs the true σ. When σ is unknown we estimate it with the sample SD, which adds uncertainty, and the T distribution (with heavier tails) accounts for that.

questions.q: H₀: μ = 1000 g. A sample of 36 packets has mean 996 g, and the machine's σ = 12 g. Two-tailed test, α = 0.05. What is z, and what is the decision?
questions.explain: SE = 12 / √36 = 2. z = (996 − 1000) / 2 = −2.0. |−2.0| > 1.96, so reject H₀: the machine is under-filling.

questions.q: In the 2 × 3 payment table, the 'New' row total is 261, the 'Cash on Delivery' column total is 145, and the grand total is 600. What is the EXPECTED count for New + COD if H₀ (independence) is true?
questions.code: E = row total × column total / grand total
questions.explain: E = 261 × 145 / 600 ≈ 63.1. The OBSERVED count was 96, far above 63.1, which is why the chi-square statistic was large (40.85).

questions.q: How many degrees of freedom does a chi-square test on a 2 × 3 contingency table have?
The ANOVA on the three delivery partners gives F = 29.77, p < 0.001. What can you conclude?
options: At least one partner's mean delivery time differs from the others
All three partners have different means from each other
ExpressGo is definitely the slowest, from the F value alone
questions.explain: ANOVA only says 'not all means are equal'. To find WHICH partners differ you look at the group means (34.3 vs 30.4 vs 29.8) and run a post-hoc test such as Tukey's HSD.

questions.q: The same 20 riders are timed on their routes before and after a training course. Which test fits best?
questions.explain: Each rider is measured twice, so the two lists are linked. A paired T-test works on each rider's difference (after − before).

questions.q: Which SciPy function runs a one-way ANOVA?
questions.explain: f_oneway → ANOVA; ttest_ind → independent T-test; chi2_contingency → chi-square test of independence; norm.cdf → area under the normal curve (used for Z-tests).

questions.q: Comparing ORDER VALUE between the old and new app gives t = −0.49, p = 0.63. What is the correct conclusion?
options: There is no evidence that the app changes order value
The test proves the two apps give exactly the same order value
The new app lowers order value
The result is significant because t is negative
questions.explain: p = 0.63 > 0.05, so we fail to reject H₀. 'No evidence of a difference' is not the same as 'proof of no difference'.

questions.q: With 2 lakh orders, a new packaging step adds 0.2 seconds to delivery and the test gives p = 0.001. What is the best interpretation?
options: Statistically significant, but too small to matter in practice
A huge effect, because the p-value is tiny
Not significant, because the effect is small
questions.explain: With very large samples even tiny differences become significant. Always report the effect size (here 0.2 s) and ask whether it matters to the business.
